MeDoc Dentist website case study · Sifra Labs
Case study · Own website
A product site in English, French and Arabic that shows the real app, real documents and prices in dirhams, with no trackers.
MeDoc Dentist needed a place where a dentist in Morocco can see the program, compare the editions and ask for a demo.

It had to read well in French and Arabic, with Arabic laid out right to left. It had to show only what the app really does, with prices in dirhams. And it had to respect visitors: no tracking, and nothing collected beyond what they choose to send.

A website with one page for each question a dentist asks: what the program does, which edition fits, what it costs, what Moroccan law says about patient data, how the program keeps that data safe, and how to get a demo.

Every screen on the site is a capture of the running app with demo data. Every sample document is a real PDF made by the app's own code: Moroccan invoices, a credit note, prescriptions and medical certificates, in French and Arabic.
The demo form sends the request to our contact service. If that service can't be reached, the visitor's own mail app opens with the message ready to send.
How the contact service works
The site is a single-page app in React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite.
It uses hash routes, such as #/pricing, so it runs on static hosting with no server of its own. Older links still open the page that now holds their section.

French is the default language. The French and Arabic copy is typed against the English, so a missing translation stops the build instead of reaching a visitor. In French and Arabic, numbers and dates follow the Moroccan format.
Arabic switches the whole layout to right to left. The theme and the text direction are set before the first paint, so the page does not flash.
Fonts are served from the site itself. There are no analytics, no third-party trackers and no third-party scripts.
The only cookies are three first-party ones, for the language, the theme and the cookie notice, written when the visitor makes a choice.
GitHub Actions builds the site. A pull request is type-checked and built but never published; a push to the main branch publishes it to GitHub Pages.
Live in English, French and Arabic, with Arabic laid out right to left.
26 screens of the real app, captured with demo data.
Real PDF documents from the app, not mock-ups.
No analytics and no third-party trackers.
Every change is type-checked and built before it goes live, and a push to the main branch publishes it with no manual steps.

sifralabs.com case study · Sifra Labs
A static company site in English, French and Arabic, with no cookies or trackers, and a contact form that falls back to your own mail app.
We needed a company site in English, French and Arabic that collects nothing it does not need and still gets every message to us.

Each extra language usually means another copy of every page to keep in step. And the contact form is often the weakest part of a small site: it attracts spam, it can send the same message twice, and when the mail server is down the message is lost.
A static site with one English source for each page. The French and Arabic pages are generated from it every time the site is built.
A contact service that receives the form, checks it and e-mails it to our mailbox. The demo form on the MeDoc Dentist website uses the same service.
The home page of sifralabs.com.
A command menu that jumps to any page from the keyboard, and pages that start loading when you point at a link, so the next one opens faster.
Vite builds plain HTML pages. Shared parts such as the header and the footer are written once and included at build time.

Translations are dictionaries keyed by the English text. The build swaps every sentence, sets Arabic pages to right to left, adds the language links, and lists any sentence that still lacks a translation.
The Content-Security-Policy only allows files from sifralabs.com itself, forbids inline styles, and stops other sites from framing the pages.
Fonts are served from the site too. There are no cookies, no analytics and no third-party scripts.
Only the contact API runs code, on a Cloudflare Worker. Every other page is served as a static file.
The Worker accepts messages only from our own sites, limits the size of every field, and strips line breaks from the fields that go into e-mail headers.
Two quiet spam traps sit in the form: a hidden field that people never fill in, and a minimum time on the page.
Each message carries an idempotency key. If you click twice or the browser retries, the Worker recognises the key for 10 minutes and sends the message only once.
The Worker sends the e-mail with Cloudflare Email Sending over an encrypted connection and does not store the message.
If the service can't be reached, your own mail app opens with the message filled in, and a button copies the text in case you prefer to paste it.
Three languages from one source, with Arabic laid out right to left.
No cookies, no analytics and no third-party scripts or fonts.
One contact service for both of our sites, with a fallback when it is down.
A double click or a retry sends one message, not two.
Security headers on every page: a Content-Security-Policy, HSTS, and a Permissions-Policy that turns off the camera, microphone, location, payment and USB.
A security.txt file that tells researchers where to report a vulnerability.
This site grows with the company. As our first client projects finish, their case studies will join our own, with each client's permission.

How MeDoc Dentist gets a practice ready
What a MeDoc program changes in a practice
These benefits come with every MeDoc program, whatever the specialty.
Patients, appointments, records, documents and payments in one program, instead of paper cards, notebooks and spreadsheets.
Your data stays in your practice
MeDoc runs on the practice's own computers, and patient records stay there. They are not sent to a cloud.
Records, appointments and invoices keep working when the connection drops, because they do not depend on it.
Made for your specialty
You do not bend generic forms to fit your work. Each MeDoc program follows the way its specialty works.
Ready for digital-health rules
Structured records, controlled access and a log of who opened which record. That is the groundwork data-protection law asks for, and a shared medical record will need.
From the first call to the months after the switch, you deal with the people who make MeDoc.
One secure core under every MeDoc program
We build the protection once, in a core that every MeDoc program shares. Each new program starts with the same safeguards instead of rebuilding them.
The practice database and every backup are encrypted on the disk where they are stored.
What each account may see and do is checked by the core itself, not only hidden on the screen.
Tamper-evident audit chain
Changes and reads of medical records go into a log. Each entry is chained to the one before, so an altered or deleted entry is detected.
Sync over the local network
The practice's computers share one encrypted database over the local network, with each change signed. In MeDoc Dentist, this comes with Cabinet and Cabinet+.
Signed licences
Each licence carries our digital signature, and the program checks it, so a forged or altered licence is refused.
Automatic encrypted backups
Once a day the core makes a compressed, encrypted backup by itself, and removes old copies on a fixed rotation so the disk does not fill up.

Why we started MeDoc with dentists

The patient card shown above is real. It comes from a Moroccan dental practice. On one sheet of paper it holds a printed tooth chart, the treatments written by hand, the prices and what has been paid. Cards like this one are why we started with dentists.

Paper has only one copy. A card can be misfiled, damaged or lost, and handwriting can be misread. When a university dental hospital in South Africa audited its records, 105 of the 362 files it wanted to review could not be found.
The rules are changing too. Bill 52-26, filed with Parliament in July 2026 and not yet law, would give every patient a shared medical record that professionals update after each consultation.
A card in a drawer cannot take part in that.

We decided that patient data should stay in the practice. MeDoc runs on the practice's own computers and works without the internet, so a cut connection does not stop the day. Data kept in the practice has to be protected there, so the database and its backups are encrypted, and every reading of a medical record is logged.
Health and social data are a real target. Moroccan media reported that the April 2025 cyberattack on the national social security fund (CNSS) exposed information on nearly 2 million people.

Software alone does not take a practice off paper. Someone has to look at how the practice works, bring the existing lists in, train the people who use it every day and answer the first questions. That is why every MeDoc program comes with the Digitalization Pack, and why the people who build MeDoc are the ones who help you switch.
